title: Ki Teitzei: build the railing (Deuteronomy 22:8)
hook: a new house needs a parapet so no one falls

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mother bird sent away, and the debate about why. Your line was spare the mother. Which creature did you treat gently? Today, from a nest to a rooftop. Day five hundred eight.

Houses in ancient Israel had flat roofs, and people used them. They dried flax up there, slept there on hot nights, ate there, talked there. In the Bible, Rahab hides the spies under flax on her roof. A roof was a room without walls. Which meant that on any warm evening, someone, a child chasing a ball, a guest who'd had a little wine, an old man stepping back to see the stars, was one step from a fall. One sentence in Ki Teitzei is about that step.
screen: `FLAT ROOFS, USED LIKE ROOMS.` → `RAHAB'S FLAX.` → `ONE STEP FROM A FALL.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "When thou buildest a new house, then thou shalt make a parapet for thy roof, that thou bring not blood upon thy house, if any man fall from thence." The Hebrew for parapet is ma'akeh: a low wall, a railing. Notice what it asks. Not that you push no one off the roof. Of course not. It asks you to think ahead about a fall that hasn't happened, to someone you may not even know yet. And if you don't, and someone falls, the verse says the blood is on your house. Not on fate. On you, the builder who could have seen it coming. The rabbis took the railing and ran with it. The Talmud, in Bava Kamma, says a person shouldn't keep a dangerous dog in the house, or leave a rickety ladder standing, because of this verse. Maimonides writes that anything on your property that puts life in danger, an open pit, an uncovered well, a weak wall, has to be fixed, and this is both a positive command and a prohibition. The roof became a stand-in for every hazard you own. There's something quietly radical in it. Most laws punish harm after it's done. This one makes prevention the commandment. It says caring for other people includes the dull work of thinking about what could go wrong in your own space, and fixing it before anyone gets hurt.
screen: `MA'AKEH: A RAILING.` · `A FALL THAT HASN'T HAPPENED YET.` · `THE DOG, THE LADDER, THE PIT.` · `PREVENTION IS THE COMMANDMENT.` · then, large: `BUILD THE RAILING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fix one hazard at home. Settle, and breathe. Walk through your home in your mind, room by room, the way a visitor might. The rug that slides. The stairs with no light. The cord across the floor. The medicine within a small child's reach. The smoke alarm with a dead battery. The pool gate, the loose step, the balcony. Go slowly. Find the one most likely to hurt someone. Picture fixing it, and decide when. The bell holds the time.
Ki Teitzei. When you go out. The portion where a new house needs a railing before anyone falls.
Your line: build the railing. Today, fix the hazard you found, or at least start: a battery, a light, a latch. Day five hundred eight.

howItsDone: Jewish law treats the railing as a real obligation: many observant Jews build a parapet around flat roofs and balconies, and the commandment is cited for home and workplace safety more broadly, including some who say a blessing when building one.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old building code.
what it means: prevention is itself the commandment: think ahead about a fall that hasn't happened, and fix it.
what a scholar hears: Bava Kamma 15b extends it to dogs and ladders; Maimonides, Laws of Murder 11:4, to every hazard, as positive and negative command.
